legacy_claims.text: Multi-agent systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) require coordination mechanisms that scale with agent count while minimizing communication overhead. Current frameworks rely on centralized orchestration patterns—Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), role hierarchies, or conversational consensus—that introduce control flow dependencies and increase latency as swarm size grows. This paper presents **Praval**, a framework implementing the **Actor Model** of computation [1] for LLM-based agent coordination. Praval replaces centralized control with message-passing between autonomous agents through a publish-substrate substrate called the **Reef**, using structured message envelopes (**Spores**) that decouple sender and receiver. In comparative evaluation against CrewAI (role-based) and LangGraph (graph-based) frameworks on an identical multi-step reasoning task, Praval reduced end-to-end latency by 90% (3.23s vs. 33.56s) and 41% (3.23s vs. 5.47s), respectively. The reduction stems from asynchronous message routing and elimination of sequential dependencies inherent in role hierarchies. We describe Praval's implementation, including a four-tier memory system (short-term, episodic, semantic, persistent vector), protocol-agnostic transport layer (AMQP, MQTT, STOMP), and OpenTelemetry-based observability. Two deployed applications—academic literature analysis and manufacturing analytics—demonstrate the framework's application to tasks requiring coordination among 5–10 agents with heterogeneous capabilities.
